summary: The Paramaras, a Rajput dynasty of Malwa, broke free of their Rashtrakuta overlords when Siyaka II sacked Manyakheta in 972, and ruled from Dhara. Munja and the scholar-king Bhoja (c. 1010–1055) made Malwa a great power and a centre of learning, but Chalukya, Kalachuri and Gujarati attacks wore it down, and from c. 1136 to c. 1175 Malwa was held by the Chaulukyas of Gujarat. Vindhyavarman restored the kingdom, which survived raids from Gujarat, the Deccan and Delhi until Alauddin Khalji's general killed the last king, Mahalakadeva, in 1305.
details: Siyaka II had made the Paramaras independent of the Rashtrakutas by sacking their capital, Manyakheta, in 972. His son Vakpati Munja, king from about 972, turned this freedom into conquest. He plundered Aghata, the capital of the Guhilas of Mewar, and the Paramaras gained eastern Mewar, including the great fort of Chittor. He also claimed victories over the Kalachuris of Tripuri, the Chahamanas, the Hunas and a Chalukya ruler of Lata, though some of these brought no new land. Munja, a poet and a patron of poets, is credited with the Munja Sagar lake at Dhar.

Munja's most dangerous rival was Tailapa II, founder of the Western Chalukya kingdom in the Deccan. The 14th-century writer Merutunga claims Munja beat Tailapa six times. Ignoring his minister's advice, Munja then crossed the Godavari to finish him off, but his army was defeated and he was taken prisoner and executed. The date falls between 994, when a text describes him as still reigning, and Tailapa's death in 998. The Chalukyas seized the southern part of the Paramara kingdom, possibly as far as the Narmada river.

Munja was succeeded by his brother Sindhuraja, not by Bhoja as later legend claimed. Sindhuraja defeated Satyashraya of the Western Chalukyas and won back the territory lost in the Deccan war. He also campaigned against the Hunas, the Somavanshis of south Kosala, the Shilaharas of the Konkan and the ruler of Lata. His court poet Padmagupta celebrated these wars in the Nava-sahasanka-charita, which also first records the legend that the Paramaras were born from a sacred fire. Historians think the poem exaggerates, but Sindhuraja left Malwa strong for his son Bhoja.

Bhoja, the most famous Paramara king, came to the throne around 1010; his earliest record, the Modasa copper plates, dates from 1010–11. Ruling from Dhara (modern Dhar), he was celebrated as a scholar-king and patron of learning. He founded the Bhojshala, a centre of Sanskrit study with a temple of Sarasvati, and is credited with founding Bhojpur, where dams held back a great lake around the Bhojeshwar Temple. Under him Dhara and Malwa became leading centres of learning, and his long reign, to about 1055, was the high point of Paramara power.

Bhoja spent much of his reign at war. Around 1018 he invaded Lata, in what is now southern Gujarat, and subjugated its Chalukya rulers. Between 1018 and 1020 he also captured the Konkan coast from the Shilaharas and celebrated with a victory festival. He joined Rajendra Chola and the Kalachuri Gangeya in an alliance against the Western Chalukya king Jayasimha II, a war in which both sides claimed victory. At its height his kingdom stretched from Chittor in the north to the upper Konkan in the south, and from the Sabarmati river in the west to Vidisha in the east.

The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani remained Bhoja's great enemy. Some time after 1042 their king Someshvara I invaded Malwa and sacked Dhara, and later Chalukya inscriptions boast of plundering Dhara, Ujjain and Mandu. Bhoja recovered his capital and his kingdom, but the war cost him his southern lands: the Konkan was lost, and the Paramara frontier moved back from the Godavari to the Narmada. Bhoja also failed against the Kachchhapaghatas of Gwalior and was checked by the Chandelas in the east, so his kingdom stopped growing.

Near the end of Bhoja's reign two neighbours joined forces against him: the Chaulukya king Bhima I of Gujarat and the Kalachuri king Karna. According to Merutunga, Bhoja refused to accept Karna's overlordship and died of disease just as the allied armies attacked, in about 1055. His successor Jayasimha I faced the invasion and may have needed help from the Chalukyas of Kalyani, his father's old enemies, to survive. Bhoja's empire did not outlive him: from now on the Paramaras were mostly defending Malwa rather than expanding it.

Bhoja's brother Udayaditya came to the throne around 1070. He repulsed a Chaulukya invasion from Gujarat under Karna, but he was also defeated by his own vassal Chamundaraja of Vagada, a sign that control over the outer Paramara lands was slipping. His successor Lakshmadeva (c. 1086–1094) was later credited with sweeping conquests in a court eulogy, but historians think these were exaggerated; at most he defeated the Kalachuris of Tripuri. The kingdom held together, but rival powers pressed on it from every side.

Under Naravarman (c. 1094–1133) the Paramaras lost wars to the Chandelas and to Jayasimha Siddharaja, the Chaulukya king of Gujarat. The war with Gujarat ended under Yashovarman, when Jayasimha, helped by Chahamana allies, captured Dhara; the historian A. K. Majumdar dates this to about 1135–36. Gujarati writers say the Malwa king was carried off in a cage, though the sources disagree on whether he was Naravarman or Yashovarman. By 1137 Jayasimha was calling himself Avantinatha, 'Lord of Avanti', and he set a governor over Ujjain. Malwa had become part of the Chaulukya realm.

Paramara rule did not vanish at once. After Jayasimha's death, Jayavarman I took the royal title and briefly regained Dhara around 1142–43, but he lost it to a usurper named Ballala. Around 1150 the new Chaulukya king Kumarapala defeated Ballala with help from the Chahamana ruler Alhana of Naddula and the Paramara chief of Abu. Malwa was now a province of Gujarat, and for about a generation the main Paramara line had no kingdom. A junior Paramara branch, the Mahakumaras, kept some lands around Bhopal.

Around 1175 Jayavarman's son Vindhyavarman defeated the king of Gujarat and re-established Paramara rule in Malwa, according to an inscription of his grandson Arjunavarman. Historians disagree about whether his opponent was the Chaulukya Mularaja II. His position was never secure: the Hoysalas and the Yadavas of Devagiri invaded from the south, and the Chaulukya general Kumara defeated him at Goggasthana. Even so, he had regained the capital, Dhara, by 1192. His son Subhatavarman, who succeeded in 1194, was strong enough to raid Gujarat in turn.

By the 13th century the Delhi Sultanate had become the strongest power in northern India. In 1233–35 (the sources differ) Sultan Iltutmish raided the Paramara cities of Bhilsa (Vidisha) and Ujjain. At Bhilsa his army occupied the city and destroyed a great temple, and at Ujjain it damaged the Mahakaleshwar temple and carried off rich plunder. Iltutmish made little effort to annex Malwa, and the Paramara king Devapala soon recaptured Bhilsa. But the raid exposed the kingdom's weakness. Squeezed by Delhi, Gujarat and the Yadavas, it lasted until 1305, when Alauddin Khalji's general killed the last king.
